div.head: III Atr 14
div.ab: And se þe sitte úncwydd ⁊ uncrafod on his áre on life, þæt nan mann on his yrfenuman ne spéce æfter his dǽge.
[14] Et qui permanet sine crauatione et calumpnia in pace sua dum uiuit, nemo super heredes eius loquatur inde post mortem.
And se þe sitte úncwydd ⁊ uncrafod on his áre on life, þæt nan mann on his yrfenuman ne spéce æfter his dǽge.
Und wer auf seinem Grundeigen bei Lebzeiten unbestritten und unbeklagt sitzt: dass nach dessen Lebzeiten niemand gegen dessen Erben klage [um dies Gut].
And whoever sits on his property in his lifetime uncontested and unchallenged: that after his day no one bring a claim [for this property] against his heir.
And if a man dwells on his property free from claims and charges during his lifetime, no-one shall bring an action against his heirs after his death.
And if anyone dwells undisturbed by charges and claims on his estates during his lifetime, no one is to bring an action against his heirs after his death.

Diesen Satz benutzt II Cn 72 = Hn 14, 5.—Auf den Missstand, der ihn hervorrief, spielt an V Atr 32, 3. Dass man den Erblasser nicht cwydde oððon crafode, antwortet Erbnehmer auf Klage um Grundbesitz; Becwæð 3, 1.—Für ar, das in anderem Zusammenhange ‘Ehre, Gunst, Gnade’ heissen kann, setzt Q, den Sinn verwässernd, ‘Frieden’ falsch

This sentence is used by II Cn 72 = Hn 14, 5. — V Atr 32, 3 alludes to the abuse that gave rise to it. In Becwæð 3, 1 the heir, answering a claim to landed property, says that no one had cwydde oððon crafode the testator. — For ar, which in another context can mean ‘honour, favour, grace’, Q wrongly puts ‘peace’, diluting the sense

Als Synonym für beide Wörter braucht V Atr 32, 3. II Cn 72, 1 beclipian. Die dem Norden entlehnte Formel (s. Wb: Alliteration, Gl Vorladung 1 Z. 11) gibt also vielleicht nur Einen Begriff; so Opet Prozesseinl. 54. Doch weist Steenstrup (Danelag 184) die Wörter kvaða und krafa in Norwegen nach als ‘Forderung in liquiden bzw. illiquiden Sachen’

V Atr 32, 3. II Cn 72, 1 use beclipian as a synonym for both words. The formula borrowed from the North (see Wb: Alliteration, Gl Vorladung 1 l. 11) thus perhaps expresses only a single concept; so Opet Prozesseinl. 54. Steenstrup (Danelag 184), however, shows that the words kvaða and krafa in Norway mean ‘claim in liquid and in illiquid matters’ respectively
